# Part B: Conditional Statements

## Question 1

```{r}
temp <- 33

if (temp >= 32) {
  print("Hot")
} else {
  print("Not hot")
}
```

**Result:** 33 is at least 32, so the test is TRUE and the first branch prints "Hot".

## Question 2

```{r}
age <- 17

if (age < 13) {
  print("Child")
} else if (age <= 19) {
  print("Teenager")
} else {
  print("Adult")
}
```

**Result:** 17 is not below 13, so the first test fails. It is within 13 to 19, so R prints "Teenager" and ignores the rest.

## Question 3

```{r}
marks  <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62)
result <- ifelse(marks >= 60, "Pass", "Fail")
print(result)
```

**Result:** ifelse() tests all five marks together. Only 45 is below 60, so the output is Fail, Pass, Pass, Pass, Pass.

## Question 4

```{r}
x <- 10

if (x > 5) {
  print("A")
} else if (x > 8) {
  print("B")
} else {
  print("C")
}
```

**Prediction:** "A". The code printed "A".

```{r}
# x > 5 is TRUE for x = 10, so R runs the first block and leaves the chain.
# "B" is never printed even though x > 8 is also true, because an
# if / else if chain only runs the FIRST branch whose test is TRUE.
```

## Question 5

`if` looks at one TRUE/FALSE value and then runs a block of code. `ifelse()` looks at every element of a vector and returns a vector with one answer per element. I use `if ... else` for a single decision, like checking whether a file exists, or when a branch has several lines of code to run. I use `ifelse()` when I am making a new column out of an existing column.

# Part C: Importing the CSV File

## Question 6

### Importing the file safely

```{r}
csv_name <- "students_grades.csv"

if (file.exists(csv_name)) {
  grades <- read.csv(csv_name, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
  cat("Imported", csv_name, "successfully.\n")
} else {
  stop("Cannot find students_grades.csv. Save it in the same folder as this .Rmd file.")
}
```

The check keeps R from trying to read a file that is not there, and it gives a clear message instead of a confusing error.

### Inspecting the data

```{r}
head(grades, 6)     # first 6 rows
dim(grades)         # rows and columns
names(grades)       # column names
str(grades)         # data types
summary(grades)     # basic statistics
colSums(is.na(grades))  # missing values per column
```

### Questions about the data

```{r}
nrow(grades); ncol(grades)
colSums(is.na(grades))[colSums(is.na(grades)) > 0]
class(grades$Section)
range(grades$Attendance)
```

1. **Size:** `grades` has `r nrow(grades)` rows and `r ncol(grades)` columns.
2. **Missing values:** The Midterm column holds the only NA, a total of `r sum(is.na(grades))`.
3. **Type of Section:** `r class(grades$Section)`, since the sections are letters.
4. **Attendance range:** The lowest is `r min(grades$Attendance)` and the highest is `r max(grades$Attendance)`.

### Sanity check

```{r}
stopifnot(nrow(grades) == 15,
          ncol(grades) == 7,
          sum(is.na(grades)) == 1)
cat("OK: 15 rows, 7 columns, one NA.\n")
```

## Applying conditional statements

### f.1 Final grade

```{r}
grades$FinalGrade <- grades$Quiz * 0.30 + grades$Midterm * 0.30 + grades$Final * 0.40
head(grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade")], 15)
```

The student without a midterm gets NA, because any calculation that includes NA gives NA.

### f.2 Pass or fail

```{r}
grades$Result <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete",
                        ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Passed", "Failed"))
table(grades$Result)
```

The NA test goes first, because `NA >= 75` returns NA instead of TRUE or FALSE.

### f.3 Remarks

```{r}
fg <- grades$FinalGrade

grades$Remarks <- ifelse(is.na(fg),  "Incomplete",
                  ifelse(fg >= 90,   "Excellent",
                  ifelse(fg >= 85,   "Very Good",
                  ifelse(fg >= 80,   "Good",
                  ifelse(fg >= 75,   "Fair",
                                     "Needs Improvement")))))
table(grades$Remarks)
```

### f.4 Attendance flag

```{r}
grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK")
table(grades$AttendanceFlag)
```

### f.5 Honors

```{r}
grades$Honors <- ifelse(!is.na(grades$FinalGrade) &
                          grades$FinalGrade >= 90 &
                          grades$Attendance >= 90,
                        "Yes", "No")
table(grades$Honors)
```

Putting `!is.na()` first guarantees that a missing final grade ends up as "No".

### f.6 if ... else if inside a loop

```{r}
loop_result <- character(nrow(grades))

for (i in 1:nrow(grades)) {
  score <- grades$FinalGrade[i]
  if (is.na(score)) {
    loop_result[i] <- "Incomplete"
  } else if (score >= 75) {
    loop_result[i] <- "Passed"
  } else {
    loop_result[i] <- "Failed"
  }
}

data.frame(Name = grades$Name, ifelse_version = grades$Result, loop_version = loop_result)
identical(grades$Result, loop_result)
```

A plain `if` handles one value at a time, so the loop feeds it one student per round. Both methods give the same result.

### f.7 A plain if on the whole column

```{r, error=TRUE}
if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed")
```

`grades$FinalGrade >= 75` produces 15 answers (one of them NA), but `if` needs exactly one TRUE or FALSE. R 4.2 and newer stops with an error about a condition of length greater than 1, while older versions only warn and use the first value. The loop version works because each round tests a single score, and the `is.na()` check comes before the comparison.

### f.8 Summary

```{r}
n_passed  <- sum(grades$Result == "Passed")
n_at_risk <- sum(grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk")
n_honors  <- sum(grades$Honors == "Yes")

c(Passed = n_passed, At_Risk = n_at_risk, Honors = n_honors)
table(grades$Result)
table(grades$AttendanceFlag)
table(grades$Honors)
```

```{r}
# Passed students:    see Passed in the output above
# At Risk students:   see At_Risk in the output above
# Honors candidates:  see Honors in the output above
```

Totals for this data set: `r n_passed` passed, `r n_at_risk` are At Risk, and `r n_honors` are honors candidates.

### f.9 Column check

```{r}
stopifnot(ncol(grades) == 12)
names(grades)
```

# Part D: Exporting Results to .csv

## Question 7

### Full processed table

```{r}
write.csv(grades, "students_grades_processed.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```

### At-risk students

```{r}
at_risk <- subset(grades, AttendanceFlag == "At Risk")

if (nrow(at_risk) >= 1) {
  write.csv(at_risk, "at_risk_students.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  cat("Wrote", nrow(at_risk), "at-risk student(s).\n")
} else {
  cat("Nobody is at risk, so no file was created.\n")
}
```

### Honors list

```{r}
honors <- grades[grades$Honors == "Yes",
                 c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance")]
honors

if (nrow(honors) >= 1) {
  write.csv(honors, "honors_list.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  cat("Wrote", nrow(honors), "honors candidate(s).\n")
} else {
  cat("No honors candidates, so no file was created.\n")
}
```

### Verifying the exports

```{r}
back_all <- read.csv("students_grades_processed.csv")
dim(back_all)
dim(grades)
all.equal(back_all, grades, check.attributes = FALSE)
```

```{r}
if (file.exists("at_risk_students.csv")) {
  back_risk <- read.csv("at_risk_students.csv")
  print(back_risk)
  cat("Same number of rows as at_risk:", nrow(back_risk) == nrow(at_risk), "\n")
}

if (file.exists("honors_list.csv")) {
  back_honors <- read.csv("honors_list.csv")
  print(back_honors)
  cat("Same number of rows as honors:", nrow(back_honors) == nrow(honors), "\n")
}
```

Reading the files back confirms that the rows, columns and values match what was written. I also opened `at_risk_students.csv` in Excel to look at it myself.

## Question 8

```{r}
back_all[is.na(back_all$FinalGrade), c("StudentID", "Name", "Midterm", "FinalGrade", "Result")]
```

The missing midterm is saved as the text `NA` in the file, and `read.csv()` converts it back into a real missing value.

Trying it without `row.names = FALSE` on a temporary file:

```{r}
write.csv(grades, "temp_check.csv")
readLines("temp_check.csv", n = 3)
ncol(read.csv("temp_check.csv"))
file.remove("temp_check.csv")
```

Without the argument, R adds an unnamed first column with the numbers 1 to 15, so the file has 13 columns instead of 12. When the file is read back, that column shows up as `X`, which is clutter the registrar does not need.

## Question 9

### a-b. Scholarship column

```{r}
grades$Scholarship <-
  ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Pending",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Full",
  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Partial",
         "None")))

grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Attendance", "Scholarship")]
```

The order matters. The missing grade is handled first. Then Full is tested before Partial, since anyone who qualifies for Full would also pass the Partial test.

### c. Students with Full or Partial

```{r}
scholars <- grades[grades$Scholarship %in% c("Full", "Partial"), ]
scholars
```

### d. Exporting with a guard

```{r}
if (nrow(scholars) > 0) {
  write.csv(scholars, "scholarship_candidates.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  cat("Wrote", nrow(scholars), "scholarship candidate(s).\n")
} else {
  cat("No one qualifies, so no file was created.\n")
}
```

### e. Count per category

```{r}
table(grades$Scholarship)
```

## Question 10

```{r}
# 1. I checked is.na() first because a comparison with NA returns NA, not
#    TRUE or FALSE. That would break if() with an error and give the student
#    with the missing score a wrong or empty label in ifelse().

# 2. If the Failed test came before the Incomplete test, the student with the
#    missing grade would not be labelled Incomplete. FinalGrade < 75 is NA for
#    that student, so the result would be NA (or an error inside an if).

# 3. ifelse() is better for building a whole column from a vector of values.
#    if ... else is better for one single decision (like checking that a file
#    exists) or when a branch needs to run several lines of code.

# 4. Reading the exported CSV back lets me confirm that the file really has the
#    right rows, columns and NA values, instead of assuming the export worked.
```
